source: Roberts, Moore, Pham, Ewaleifoh, Fisher (2024) Large Language Model Recall Uncertainty is Modulated by the Fan Effect (CoNLL)
finding: First direct test of Anderson's fan effect in LLMs. Fan shows up in token probabilities (not in accuracy), and only when the model is unsure. When the queried item is truly absent, the probability of saying 'absent' is lower for items with higher fan (more typical items, or more in-context repeats). When the item is present and the model is sure, the fan effect vanishes.
numbers: Pretraining-fan experiment: 10 Rosch categories, half of items per category in a list; Mistral and SOLAR show significant negative Pearson correlations (r beyond 0.3) between typicality and canary probability for absent items. RoBERTa, GPT-2, Llama-2 showed no significant correlation; Llama-3 a slight one. In-context experiment (Anderson 1974 recreation): 20 persons x 20 places, 16 fan combinations, population of N=50 perturbed models per base model (PopulationLM), Mistral and SOLAR only. Absent-item queries: all correlations with fan significant (p<=0.01); present-item queries: none significant.
quote: with uncertainty mitigated, the observed fan effect is disrupted
limits: Only 2 of 6 models show it. Population variance showed no effect (only token probability does). Effect is on probability, not on measured recall errors. Person-fan gave effects; place-fan disrupted or reversed them (SOLAR had a positive correlation), matching human differential-fan findings only loosely. Noise floors (0.2-0.45) used to filter data. Small 7B-10.7B models.
agent_relevance: Fan in an LLM is an uncertainty signal, not a hard failure: crowded cues make the model less sure about absence and presence. Supports using confidence on 'is X in memory' as a diagnostic, but not as proof of retrieval failure.

source: Huang et al. (2025) Analyzing Memory Effects in Large Language Models through the lens of Cognitive Psychology (arXiv 2509.17138v2)
finding: Ran the Schneider and Anderson person-location recognition paradigm on GPT-4 (gpt-4-0125-preview), Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and LLaMA-3-8B. Accuracy falls when each person or location appears in 2 facts instead of 1 (fan 2 vs fan 1), and d-prime is lower for fan 2. Same sign as in humans.
numbers: Study list of 32 person-location facts, fan 1 vs fan 2, foil list rearranged with fan kept equal. For the main model accuracy fell from 0.991 (fan 1) to 0.915 (fan 2). d' lower for Fan 2 in all lag groups. Offline 7-8B models showed the same direction with more noise.
quote: when the fan value increases, the recall accuracy of the language model ... shows a negative relationship
limits: Only fan 1 vs 2, one list size for the fan test, no replication count or significance test reported in the text I read; the 'fan effect' here is accuracy not reaction time. Ceiling effects (0.99). Recall tasks were near perfect; effect only in recognition. Positional effect absent in LLMs (unlike humans).
agent_relevance: Small, clean confirmation that even a short in-context list shows fan cost in recognition. Fan 1 to 2 costs about 8 points in a strong model, so even a modest number of facts per cue is not free.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length (PI-LLM)
finding: Stream of key-value updates where the same key is overwritten many times and only the last value is queried. The old values for the same key are a cue-overload load. Retrieval accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as updates per key rise, for all tested models. Errors are mostly earlier values of the same key.
numbers: 46 keys, 400 words per category dictionary; update count per key 3 to 400. Log-linear decline in every model (about 30+ models; regression N=30). Parameter size class predicts resistance (t=3.03, p=0.005, N=30); context length does not (t=-0.144, p=0.886); R2=0.261. Within models of 128k-131k context, Spearman between size and score rho=0.673, p=0.0016. Value length 1 to 10 words drops accuracy under 40% for every model; 40 words under 5%.
quote: retrieval accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero as interference accumulates
limits: Synthetic key-value task with random words. Reasoning models excluded for latency (over 200 s). Sequential (non-shuffled) updates show a step-like cliff instead of a smooth log line. Humans reportedly plateau; the human comparison is cited, not run here. Later study (c11) finds the size effect weaker.
agent_relevance: The key quantitative law for our library: more same-cue entries means worse retrieval of the latest one, roughly log of entry count. Keep one current entry per cue; do not leave superseded entries in the visible window.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) PI-LLM, controls for input length and number of keys
finding: Three controls show it is interference and not length. Raising the number of keys at fixed updates per key gives a log-linear drop. Fixing the whole input (46 keys) and only asking for a subset of keys (tracked keys 1 to 46) gives almost the same log-linear curve. So the number of items you must retrieve at once, not only the amount of text, is the load.
numbers: Updates per key fixed at 125 or 350; updated keys U 1 to 46 (Exp A); tracked keys T 1 to 46 with input length constant (Exp B). Both give near-identical log-linear declines; larger models decline more slowly.
limits: Authors' wording is that the two curves are 'nearly identical', no formal equivalence test seen. Same synthetic task.
agent_relevance: Asking an agent to recall many things from one crowded context in a single step is itself a load. Query one cue at a time, or one small group, instead of all at once.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) PI-LLM, prompt-based mitigation tests
finding: Tried five inline instructions: per-key 'forget all previous updates to X', forward focus, and others (Figure 11). Gains were marginal. Telling the model to forget does not release the interference. Also, asking the model to first restate the task goal did not change the log-linear trend.
numbers: Interventions inserted about 120 updates before the end or one third before the final update; paper reports only marginal accuracy improvement; exact per-intervention gains not extracted by me.
limits: I did not capture the numeric gain per prompt. Tested on the same synthetic task and a limited model set.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'ignore the old values' prompts (fits guardrail that written instructions are weak). Remove the old entries in code instead.

source: Guo, Wu, Yiu (2026) The Interference Gap: Comparing Retrieval Bounds in Human Memory and RAG Systems (arXiv 2606.28327)
finding: Fits accuracy against fan with one log law, d'(F) = d0 - (b/sigma) ln F, for humans and for retrievers (not LLM readers). Humans lose less per log-unit of fan than dense passage retrieval. HippoRAG sits near humans.
numbers: Humans N=112 (Prolific, 120 recruited): accuracy 91.2% (fan 1), 82.4% (fan 2), 71.8% (fan 4); d' 2.84, 2.21, 1.67; Cohen d 1.12; slope 0.41 [0.35,0.47]. DPR slope 0.67 [0.58,0.76], accuracy 94.1, 76.3, 58.2, 44.7 at fan 1,2,4,8. ColBERTv2 0.53, HippoRAG 0.44 [0.37,0.51]. Log beats power law (BIC diff 15.7 to 23.1). Only human-DPR contrast is clear; HippoRAG and ColBERTv2 CIs overlap humans.
quote: Both systems show logarithmic accuracy decline with association count (fan)
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed; the arXiv number 2606 and the stated date 9 May 2026 do not match, so treat provenance with care. Human fan stops at 4, RAG goes to 8. Person-location sentences, small retrievers (DPR, ColBERTv2, HippoRAG) and no LLM readers. Authors say mechanism claims (encoding specificity, gating) are untested.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready slope for planning: each doubling of items per cue costs roughly 10 points in a human and 17 points in plain dense retrieval. Suggests retrieval over a graph of distinct entities holds up better than flat embedding search.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The Power of Noise: Redefining Retrieval for RAG Systems (SIGIR)
finding: Adding high-scoring but wrong passages (hard distractors) to the gold passage lowers answer accuracy steadily. Adding random unrelated passages did not hurt and often helped.
numbers: NQ-open, 10K queries, Llama2-7b: baseline gold only 0.5642. With ADORE hard-negative distractors, 1/2/4 distractors gave 0.4068/0.3815/0.3626. With 18 distractors and gold near / mid / far: 0.37 / 0.23 / 0.17. Random noise: best setting +0.08 (+36%) for one model; attention entropy about 3x higher with random docs.
quote: progressive accuracy degradation as the number of distracting documents
limits: Small 2023 models (Llama2-7b, Phi-2, MPT, Falcon); Falcon did not benefit from random docs. Random-doc benefit is not understood and may not hold with modern models. Gold-only 'oracle' setup.
agent_relevance: Similar-but-wrong items per cue hurt; unrelated items do not. So the harmful load is the semantically near entries sharing the cue, which maps to cue overload and not to raw library size.

source: Chattaraj and Raj (2026) LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: Dual-Process Interference in Large Language Models (arXiv 2603.00270)
finding: 39 LLMs (1B to 2.5T parameters), same stimuli, query either the first value (retroactive interference, RI) or the latest (PI). PI hurts far more than RI in every model, the reverse of the usual human result. RI errors are 'nothing returned'; PI errors are same-key intrusions of older values.
numbers: PI vs RI Cohen d=1.73; 39/39 models have RIES>PIES; mean gap 69.5 points. At N=3 mean accuracy 93.9%; RI near ceiling to N=50 (96.0%) then 25% at N=300; PI falls from 94% to 3%. Size explains 49% of RI variance (p<0.0001) but PI R2=0.06 (p=0.14). RI vs PI correlation r=0.21 (CI -0.11 to 0.49). Errors: RI 50.8% retrieval failure; PI 56.1% same-key intrusion; hallucination 0.9% (RI), 0.2% (PI). o1: RIES 186.4 (rank 1), PIES 22.0 (rank 35). Reasoning models RIES 178.0 vs 150.3.
limits: Preprint. Same synthetic key-value design as c03; contradicts c03 on whether size predicts PI resistance (authors blame MoE models with inflated parameter counts). Interference levels up to 300 updates.
agent_relevance: The stale-entry problem is worse than the 'first entry' problem. Reasoning models do not escape it. Supports a rule that the library overwrites, not appends, when a cue's value changes.

source: Qiao et al. (2026) Diagnosing Retrieval Bias Under Multiple In-Context Knowledge Updates in LLMs (DKI, arXiv 2603.12271)
finding: Frames same-fact multi-updates as the AB-AC paradigm and cites Watkins and Watkins 1975. Earliest-state accuracy stays near ceiling while latest-state accuracy collapses as updates T rise. Gap grows fast from T=32 to 128 then plateaus by T=256. Internal attention and logit signals get flat on errors.
numbers: 13 LLMs on synthetic DKIs (T=32 to 512, 200 instances) and 164 real-world DKIs (mean length 8.77). Earliest accuracy about 98-100%. Gap often above 0.6 for small and mid models; LLaMA3.1-405B, GPT5-N, Gemini2.5-F smaller; DeepSeek-V3 and Claude Sonnet 4 in between. Gap still about 91% for LLaMA3.1-8B after interventions.
limits: Synthetic text weakens semantic and prior knowledge; internal diagnostics are correlational and cover few model families.
agent_relevance: Even with only about 9 updates in real data the bias shows. Short histories of changing facts per cue are already risky.

source: Qiao et al. (2026) DKI, cognitively inspired prompt interventions
finding: Tested prompts borrowed from memory research: rote rehearsal, semantic elaboration, memory integration, directed forgetting, versus CoT, 2-shot and index numbering. Memory integration and 2-shot helped most but none removed the bias. Index numbering made things worse.
numbers: Latest-state accuracy examples (real-world set): 2-shot LLaMA3.1-8B 4.50% to 8.67%, LLaMA3.1-70B 72.17% to 76.50%, Qwen2.5-72B 55.33% to 66.67%. Index strategy dropped LLaMA3.1-70B to 38.33% and Qwen2.5-72B to 27.00%. Memory integration Qwen2.5-7B 18.67% to 25.83%, Qwen3-235B 80.67% to 86.17%. Directed forgetting Qwen2.5-32B 57.33% to 58.33%.
limits: Gains are single-digit to low-teens points; only Qwen and Llama families on the intervention table. Authors suggest numbering adds interfering tokens.
agent_relevance: Prompt tricks give a few points at most. Merging entries for the same cue into one current statement (integration) is the best of the prompt options and matches doing it in code.

source: Shahrabi-Farahani and Rahmati (2026) Compress and Forget: bitsandbytes Quantization Amplifies Proactive Interference in LLMs (arXiv 2608.18578)
finding: 4-bit quantization lowers retrieval under semantically similar overwrites for Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Phi-3.5-mini. The effect disappears or reverses with numeric attributes, so it is specific to semantic crowding. INT8 carries a smaller real penalty in two models.
numbers: Qwen: 81.0% (FP16) to 68.3% (INT4) at high interference; McNemar p<=2.6e-6. Mistral at level 16: 44.0% to 37.4%; Phi: 61.8% to 54.0%. Same-key intrusion errors 21.5% to 24.6% of trials (p=4.8e-7). Normalised IES loss INT4: 1.8% (Qwen), 5.1% (Mistral), 5.2% (Phi). Interference levels k=1 to 96.
limits: Three small open models, one quantization library, preprint. Authors cite a 39-model study (c08) for PI robustness.
agent_relevance: Cue overload sensitivity is a model-quality property, so a cheaper or compressed model needs a smaller library per cue.

source: Xie (2026) Learning to Forget: Sleep-Inspired Memory Consolidation for Resolving PI in LLMs (SleepGate, arXiv 2603.14517)
finding: Proposes learned forgetting plus merge of superseded KV-cache entries. In a toy transformer it resolves PI where five cache baselines fail. Gate fails when many near-identical entries share one entity.
numbers: 4-layer 793K-parameter transformer, PI-LLM-style benchmark: 99.5% at PI depth 5, 97.0% at depth 10; all five baselines (full cache, sliding window, H2O, StreamingLLM, decay-only) below 18%. Depth 1 anomaly 82.5%. Stale retrieval 3.5% for n<=10, 23.5-62.0% for n=15-30; accuracy 16.5% at n=30.
limits: Proof of concept at tiny scale, proposal paper, no pretrained LLM, no natural text; theoretical O(n) to O(log n) claim not tested. Depth saturates beyond n about 15.
agent_relevance: Shows the fix class that works is removing or merging stale entries before retrieval, not prompting. Same break point (about 15 near-identical entries per entity) suggests keeping per-cue lists short.

source: Li et al. (2025) Sculptor: Empowering LLMs with Cognitive Agency via Active Context Management (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2508.04664)
finding: Gives an LLM agent tools to fragment, fold (summarise/hide), restore and search its own context, aimed at proactive interference. Zero-shot with frontier models helps on multi-needle tasks and PI-LLM only modestly; RL training on a 13B model helps a lot.
numbers: Zero-shot (benchmark-specific prompts): Claude-4-Sonnet NeedleBench-M-RS avg 67.0 to 94.0 (+27); GPT-4.1 +23; DeepSeek-V3 +8. PI-LLM average gains: Claude-4-Sonnet +5.90, GPT-4.1 +6.58, DeepSeek-V3 -0.12. Claude-4-Sonnet PI-LLM per length: 4/1K 99.13 to 90.43 (worse), 64/16K 65.22 to 87.39, 256/64K 69.57 to 77.83. M3 13B baseline PI-LLM 22.5; with RAG 17.9; MemAgent 41.5; Sculptor-M3 71.8; Sculptor-M3-RL 99.4. NeedleBench M3: 30.0 / 12.5 (RAG) / 67.6 / 84.8 (RL).
limits: Needs benchmark-specific prompts for good tool use; unified generic prompt gave poor tool patterns. Self-trained M3 base model. Tool use hurt short contexts. Different tasks carry the RL gain, not clearly shown for held-out ones.
agent_relevance: One of the few agent-loop methods that acts on PI. Hide-and-restore of old context beats plain RAG here (RAG made the 13B PI-LLM score worse, 22.5 to 17.9), so more retrieval is not the fix for crowded cues.

source: Ding et al. (2026) Controlled Memory Interference in Continual LLM Agents (CMI, arXiv 2608.07622)
finding: Agent-memory probe that separates memory load from memory relationship. Piling on unrelated memories matters little; repeated history or same-slot conflicts (same cue, new value) sharply cut update uptake. Cites Watkins and Watkins 1975 in its references.
numbers: TravelPlanner, load levels L0 to L6 = 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 90, 135 memories; noise-only: plasticity 0.510 to 0.455, non-monotonic. At count 8, lexical (BM25) plasticity change vs unrelated: repeated history -0.32 (CI -0.46, -0.20), same-slot conflict -0.48 (CI -0.62, -0.34); unrelated -0.02. Dense (Qwen3-Embedding-8B): unrelated -0.18, repeated -0.46, same-slot -0.44. Dense same-slot conflict cuts stability 0.92 to 0.54. Lexical same-slot Target Recall@3 0.34; dense repeated history recall 0.48.
limits: Preprint, synthetic transformations of benchmark data, 50 base scenarios for the mechanism study. Most numbers from a TravelPlanner build.
agent_relevance: Strongest agent-memory evidence for the cue-overload point: 135 unrelated memories cost little, 8 same-slot ones cost a lot. Count of entries per cue, not library size, is what to cap.

source: Lee et al. (2026) MINTEval: Evaluating Memory under Multi-Target Interference in Long-Horizon Agent Systems (arXiv 2605.18565)
finding: 15.6K questions over contexts averaging 138.8K tokens (up to 1.8M) with about 86 updates deep. Full context, RAG, HippoRAG, MemAgent, AtomMem and others all score low. Adding distractors lowers RAG accuracy; full context less affected by distractor type.
numbers: Average accuracy 27.7% in the text (abstract says 27.9%) across systems with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B; best system average 33.4%; simple most-recent questions 47.5% average, much lower for history and aggregation. MemAgent 85.7% on bAbI Simple but 7.5% on HorizonBench. SimpleMem with Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite 30.3 EM. Retrieval and memory construction explains the main loss (evidence present in 58.3% of cases; answering adds a 25.2% drop). Memory agents insert in 76.8% of operations, rarely delete or update.
limits: Preprint; abstract and body disagree by 0.2 points; different backbone models across rows.
agent_relevance: Real agent memory systems mostly add and rarely delete, which is exactly the cue-overload-causing behavior. Update and delete operations are the missing piece.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) SYNAPSE: Empowering LLM Agents with Episodic-Semantic Memory via Spreading Activation (arXiv 2601.02744)
finding: Uses the ACT-R fan effect as a design feature: activation sent from a node is divided by its out-degree (fan), plus time decay and lateral inhibition. Ablating the fan term hurts open-domain and multi-hop questions.
numbers: LoCoMo, GPT-4o-mini: weighted F1 40.5, +7.2 over A-Mem (33.3); Temporal F1 50.1 vs 45.9; adversarial F1 96.6. Removing fan: Open-Domain F1 25.9 to 16.8. 814 tokens per query vs 16,910 for full context (95% fewer); cost $0.24 per 1,000 queries vs $2.66-2.67. Spreading factor S=0.8; temporal decay 0.01; top-k stable for k 20-40.
limits: Single benchmark (LoCoMo), single backbone for the headline; no human comparison; hub nodes handled by fan-division, lateral inhibition can cause tunneling on simple queries.
agent_relevance: Working example of fan used as a retrieval design rule rather than a bug: share a cue's activation across its entries so hub cues do not swamp results.

source: Modarressi et al. (2025) NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching (ICML 2025)
finding: When question and answer share no words, long-context accuracy falls steeply with length. Adding a distractor sentence that shares words with the question but is irrelevant makes the drop much worse. Literal overlap acts like a cue that points to the wrong item.
numbers: GPT-4o base score 99.3, falls to 69.7 at 32K; 10 of 12 models below 50% of base at 32K. GPT-4o 64K/128K retained above 50% of base at 128K; Gemini 2.0 Flash 16.4% at 128K. With a literal-overlap distractor, GPT-4o effective length drops to 1K, Llama 3.3 70B worse (base scores 93.8 and 84.4).
limits: Single needle with one inserted distractor, not a count sweep. Effective length defined at 85% of base. Models tested were early 2025.
agent_relevance: Confirms that wrong matches to the cue words are the main cost, supporting search by meaning plus a check that the returned item answers the query, not only string match.

source: Sahai Srivastava (2026) Causal Intervention-Based Memory Selection for Long-Horizon LLM Agents (CAUSAL-LOCOMO, arXiv 2605.17641)
finding: Selects memories by testing their effect on the answer (swap-in/out interventions) instead of by similarity. Top-3 similar memories are often irrelevant, stale, or misleading; vector and reflection memory adopt poisoned memories.
numbers: Final model GPT-4.1, judge GPT-5. CMI task score 0.846 and success rate 0.816, bad-memory rejection 0.990, useful-memory F1 0.875. Best baselines: reflection 0.845, vector 0.839 (about equal on task score, but they adopt poisoned memories with 3 memories selected on average).
limits: Self-built synthetic benchmark with injected harmful memories; task-score gap to baselines tiny (0.846 vs 0.845); cost of the interventions not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Shows a selection step that tests candidates against the answer. The gain is in robustness to bad memories, not accuracy, so it is a safety layer for crowded cues.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle (TACL), as cited by Guo et al. 2026
finding: Positional baseline for context retrieval. As reported in the c06 paper, items in the middle of a long context are retrieved about 20 percentage points worse than items at either end.
numbers: About 20 percentage points (secondary report in c06). Not read in this session.
limits: Secondary citation only; I did not open the original.
agent_relevance: Position and count of competing entries both matter; place the current entry for a cue at the end.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The Power of Noise, positional result
finding: Position of the gold passage interacts with how many hard distractors are present. With 18 distractors, gold nearest the query is best and gold in the middle is worst.
numbers: Llama2 with 18 distractors: near 0.37, far 0.23, mid 0.17.
limits: Same single-model, 2023-era setup as c07.
agent_relevance: Order the retrieved set so the best entry sits last, next to the question.

source: Roberts et al. (2024) Fan effect paper, positive and negative evidence on method
finding: Fan correlates with the person feature but not the place feature, which matches human differential fan effects only partly. Authors tie fan to typicality (the fan effect is a special case of typicality, as in COBWEB models) and argue LLMs learn human-like uncertainty.
numbers: SOLAR: significant negative correlation with person fan on absent items but positive correlation with place fan; Mistral negative for person fan, disrupted for place fan.
limits: Interpretive claims go beyond the correlations; does not show any recall error rise.
agent_relevance: Which feature carries the fan matters. Fan should be counted on the cue that the query actually uses.

source: Huang et al. (2025) memory effects paper, comparison with humans on fan and nonsense
finding: Across seven memory effects, LLMs match humans on list length, list strength, fan and false memory, but not position effect (flat) or nonsense effect (robust). Offline 7-8B models always trail the online model, and recall (not recognition) is near perfect.
numbers: GPT-4 hit rate on position task near perfect at all positions; offline models also perfect on position; offline models recognise lure words as new (poor generalisation). Models: gpt-4-0125-preview, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, LLaMA-3-8B.
limits: Aggregated counts without stated significance tests in text I read; person-location sentences only.
agent_relevance: Fan-type cost shows in recognition ('is this fact stored?') more than in direct recall, so test both when auditing our library.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) PI-LLM, three-stage error pattern
finding: As interference rises, errors move from adjacent earlier updates (stage 1), to far-upstream updates (stage 2), to values never shown (hallucination, stage 3) with a persistent pull to the earliest bin.
numbers: 11 equal bins over the update sequence; hallucination share small but grows with load. Chattaraj (c08) later measures hallucination at only 0.2% of PI errors.
limits: Stage description is descriptive; the two papers differ on hallucination rate.
agent_relevance: A wrong answer to a crowded cue is usually an old true value, so an old-value check against a version log can catch many errors.

source: Chattaraj and Raj (2026), metacognitive signal and bimodality
finding: Under PI, 8.6% of retrieval failures contain an explicit refusal versus 0% under RI. Under high PI the accuracy flips bimodally between near-ceiling and near-floor across runs, a winner-take-all pattern, while RI decays smoothly.
numbers: 8.6% explicit refusal in PI failures; adaptive bootstrap with 95% CI width under 0.10, at least 5 sessions, up to 50 (20 for reasoning models).
limits: LLM-as-judge for refusal; bimodality shown only at high interference.
agent_relevance: At high load the same prompt can succeed or fail by chance. Sample twice with fresh order, and treat disagreement as a sign of overload (agrees with the schema rule on disagreement as a signal).

source: Wang and Sun (2025) PI-LLM, sequential versus shuffled updates
finding: If updates arrive strictly in order for each key, accuracy stays near perfect until a model-specific threshold then drops to near zero in a step. Shuffled interleaving gives the smooth log-linear drop.
numbers: Threshold is higher for larger models in the same family; exact thresholds not extracted.
limits: Threshold values not recorded by me.
agent_relevance: Cue-grouped order may help up to a cliff; plan a hard cap on per-cue entries rather than trusting graceful decline.

source: Ding et al. (2026) CMI, update authority and retrieval pathways
finding: Recency alone does not stop an agent from accepting an invalid older memory; framing it as a persistent update or with authoritative correction wording raises acceptance. Lexical and dense retrievers fail in different ways.
numbers: Poison acceptance at fixed L3 with recency cues P0/P1: lexical .02/.02, dense .00/.00. Persistent-update framing .23 (lexical) /.12 (dense); authoritative wording .26/.14.
limits: Synthetic TravelPlanner transformation; small acceptance rates.
agent_relevance: Store a version and an authority tag on each entry for a cue; do not rely on 'newest wins' wording.

source: Watkins and Watkins (1975) Buildup of proactive inhibition as a cue-overload effect; Anderson (1974); Anderson and Reder (1999) (background cited by c06 and c09)
finding: Original human work that the LLM papers import: Watkins and Watkins 1975 explain buildup of proactive inhibition as many items sharing one cue; Anderson 1974 fan effect; Anderson and Reder 1999 review. Qiao (c09) and Ding (c14) cite Watkins 1975 directly in their reference lists; Guo (c06) cites Anderson 1974 and Anderson and Reder 1999 for the log-fan rule.
limits: I did not open these originals in this session; the human numbers belong to angle A and B files.
agent_relevance: Common-cause note: LLM PI tests are cue-overload tests (same cue, more targets). Keep citations to Watkins for the mechanism, not for LLM numbers.

source: Guo et al. (2026) Interference Gap, serial position results for retrievers
finding: Dense retrieval shows primacy, humans show recency, HippoRAG is balanced. Competitor sensitivity: DPR 0.058, ColBERTv2 0.043, HippoRAG 0.024, humans 0.021.
numbers: DPR position 1 89.2%, position 10 61.4%, position 20 68.3%; recency/primacy ratio humans 1.43, DPR 0.52, HippoRAG 0.89; human-DPR competitor contrast t=4.32, p<.001.
limits: Same caveats as c06; HippoRAG CI overlaps humans.
agent_relevance: Retriever choice changes the order effects the agent sees; do not assume the fan slope and the order effects come from one cause.
